clinical_knowledge.topic: Infective Endocarditis (Native Mitral Valve) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Infective Endocarditis (Native Mitral Valve) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes prolonged pathogen-directed IV antibiotic therapy (typically 4 weeks for penicillin-susceptible viridans streptococci) guided by blood culture susceptibilities, with early echocardiography to assess vegetation size, valve destruction, and surgical indications, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: prolonged fever, night sweats, heart murmur, and painful nodules on fingers after dental work
Key HPI features: 46M presenting with spiking fevers 4 weeks post-dental cleaning, new mitral regurgitation murmur, Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, and blood cultures positive for S. viridans.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: Temp 38.9C, HR 96, BP 118/74, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air. New holosystolic murmur at the cardiac apex radiating to the axilla (mitral regurgitation). Tender Osler nodes on finger pulps, painless Janeway lesions on palms, splinter hemorrhages under the nail beds, mild splenomegaly. Bloods: WBC 12,500 /uL, ESR 68 mm/hr, CRP elevated. Three sets of blood cultures positive for penicillin-susceptible Streptococcus viridans. Transthoracic echocardiogram shows a 9mm mobile vegetation on the mitral valve with moderate mitral regurgitation, meeting modified Duke criteria for definite infective endocarditis.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Infective Endocarditis (Native Mitral Valve).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Rheumatic fever without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: New or changing heart murmur with fever — assume endocarditis until proven otherwise.
management_principles: Obtain three sets of blood cultures from different venipuncture sites before starting antibiotics, then start IV Penicillin G (3-4 million units IV q4h) or Ceftriaxone 2g IV once daily for penicillin-susceptible Streptococcus viridans, typically for 4 weeks

Order a transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE); proceed to transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) if TTE is non-diagnostic or suspicion remains high, to characterize vegetation size/mobility and valve damage
Obtain early cardiology and cardiothoracic surgery consultation; valve surgery is indicated for heart failure, uncontrolled infection, vegetation > 10mm with embolic events, or perivalvular abscess
Arrange dental evaluation once stable and counsel on antibiotic prophylaxis before future high-risk dental procedures
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Infective Endocarditis Native Mitral Valve
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for prolonged fever, night sweats, heart murmur, and painful nodules on fingers after dental work
Select appropriate laboratory and imaging studies for infectious_disease
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies

teaching.one_liner: Bacteria — often from a dental procedure — seed a native heart valve, causing prolonged fever, a new murmur, and peripheral immune stigmata like Osler's nodes and Janeway lesions.
red_flags: New or changing heart murmur with fever — assume endocarditis until proven otherwise
Signs of embolic stroke or splenic infarct

must_ask.say: Have you had any dental work or other procedures in the past month or two?
How long have you had fevers, and do they come and go?
Have you noticed any painful bumps on your fingers or spots on your palms?
Do you have any known heart valve problems?
Have you had night sweats or unintentional weight loss?

history.answer: I've had a fever that just won't go away for the past four weeks, and I keep waking up drenched in night sweats.
The fever started about four weeks ago, roughly a few days after I had an intensive dental cleaning.
My temperature spikes up to around 39 degrees Celsius, mainly in the late afternoons, and I get severe shaking chills.
I took over-the-counter acetaminophen, but the fever keeps bouncing right back after a few hours.
About a week ago, I developed these painful red lumps on the tips of my fingers that really hurt whenever I touch anything.
I also noticed small, flat, painless red spots on the palms of my hands and dark streaks under my fingernails.
No, I haven't had any cough, phlegm, sore throat, or shortness of breath.
No burning when I urinate, no need to go more frequently, and no flank pain.
No abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea at all.
I've had a mild dull headache with the high fevers, but no severe headache, stiff neck, or confusion.
Aside from the spots and lumps on my hands, I haven't had any body rashes, bug bites, or black scabs.
Yes, I wake up soaked through my nightclothes almost every night, and I've unintentionally lost about three kilograms this month.
No, I haven't noticed any swollen lumps in my neck, armpits, or groin.
No recent international travel, no outdoor hiking or farming, and no exposure to pets or livestock.
No, no one around me at home or at my office has been sick with any fever or infection.
No, I have never received chemotherapy, and I don't take steroids or any immune-suppressing drugs.
I had a deep dental cleaning four weeks ago, and my gums bled quite a bit during the procedure.
A physician mentioned many years ago that I had a faint heart murmur, but said it was benign and I never had problems.
No, I haven't started taking any new prescription drugs, supplements, or herbal remedies.
I've been monogamous with my wife for fifteen years, and I have never injected illicit or recreational drugs.
I have no history of chronic health problems like high blood pressure, diabetes, or kidney disease.
I have never undergone surgery and have never been admitted to a hospital before.
I am not on any regular prescription medications or vitamins.
I don't have any known allergies to penicillin, other antibiotics, or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I only drink socially, having one or two beers on the weekend.
I work full-time in an office setting and live in an apartment with my wife.
There is no family history of heart disease, valve problems, or autoimmune conditions.
I thought I just caught a really stubborn strain of the flu that's been lingering in my system for weeks.

I've used up almost all my sick leave, and I'm really worried my employer is going to let me go if I miss more work. I'm hoping you can give me some heavy-duty antibiotics today so I can finally break this fever and get back to work.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, pulse 96 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, temperature 38.9°C (102.0°F), and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Patient appears fatigued and flushed with mild diaphoresis, resting comfortably without acute respiratory distress.
Conjunctivae demonstrate mild pallor without petechiae; sclerae are non-icteric.
Oral cavity is moist and pink without mucosal erythema, petechial hemorrhages, or dental caries.
No lymphadenopathy appreciated in the cervical, supraclavicular, or submandibular regions.
Tachycardic regular rhythm with a new grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur heard loudest at the apex with radiation to the left axilla.
Breath sounds are clear and equal bilaterally with no crackles, wheezes, or pleural rubs.
Abdomen is soft, non-distended, and non-tender throughout without involuntary guarding or rigidity.
Mild splenomegaly with the spleen tip palpated 2 cm below the left costal margin; liver edge is smooth and non-tender.
Tender erythematous nodules on the finger pulps (Osler nodes), non-tender macular lesions on the palms (Janeway lesions), and splinter hemorrhages under the nail beds.
Supple neck with full passive flexion; negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs.
